newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS- Dlr/yen vols firm as spot pierces 118 yen.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS- Dlr/yen vols firm as spot pierces 118 yen.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar/yen options were firmer across the curve in U.S. trading as spot rallied past 118.00 yen, the highest level since it tumbled toward 110 yen in early June, traders said.

Big hedge-fund buying of long-dated yen puts in the past several days was having a hangover effect in a seasonally thin market as many bank dealers had become short vega, in the higher strike prices, traders said.
"As we get closer (to the strike prices around 125 yen), the vega risk starts to become pretty unpleasant," said Alan Revercomb, options strategist at I.D.E.A.
Implied volatility for one-month dollar/yen rose to 11.3/11.5 percent from 10.9/11.2 late on Monday. One-year also rose a quarter point to 11.8/12.0.

Kyoko Hiramatsu, a senior dealer at Bank of Yokohama in New York, said the dollar crossed above its 200-day moving average, which came in at 117.98 yen today, and there was growing demand to rebuild positions in the upside strikes.

"It doesn't look like people have big negative-gamma risks, given the relatively mild reaction in the short dates," she said. "They, in general, seem to be putting on positions in anticipation of a higher dollar."
Shorter-dated options have higher gamma, which gives quicker premium acceleration and bigger delta swings for volatility traders.
Dollar/mark volatilities softened, particularly the front end, as spot pulled back toward 1.83 marks, from Monday's 7-1/2 year highs near 1.85, before bouncing back up slightly.
One-month dollar/mark fell to 10.0/10.3 percent versus 10.4/10.7 late on Monday.
"Part of the subdued nature of dollar/mark vols lately was because there haven't been delta-hedging opportunities," Revercomb said. "It's been such a one-way move."

Delta-neutral volatility traders, when they are long gamma, sell dollars as spot moves higher and buy dollars as spot falls. Their positions become profitable when gains from buying spot at lower levels and selling at higher levels beat the options' time decay and exceed the premiums paid.

"Today's been one of the first opportunities to really trade both ways," Revercomb said. "But one day isn't going to change that (weakness in volatilities). From a gamma trading perspective, it's probably going to have to get back below 1.83 marks and look like...there's going to be a massive correction or a volatile five-six point (pfennig) range."
Revercomb also noted that sterling, which had had a one-way bull run against most currencies earlier in the month, turned down sharply this week, spiking up volatilities.
"It's partly because of the one-day reaction, but also when you get markets at extremes like this, traders tend to be on the edge for the big turning point," he said.
One-month sterling/mark stood at 11.2/11.6 percent versus 10.7/11.1 at the end of last week. Spot was floundering below 3.00 mark after touching a 3.0878 high last week.
Revercomb said dollar/mark could follow sterling's footsteps because there was so much room for correction.
